video_title: Dino Mavrookas: America Needs to Build Ships Again
gist: Saronic CEO Dino Mavrookas lays out the scale of the US-China shipbuilding gap (230-to-1 overall, driven mainly by commercial shipbuilding) and details how his $9B+ valued, VC-backed autonomous shipbuilder is racing to rebuild US maritime industrial capacity via Navy contracts, a new Texas mega-shipyard, and a bet that the entire maritime industry -- not just defense -- shifts to autonomy.

insights.claim: China outbuilds the United States in shipbuilding by roughly 230-to-1 overall, a gap driven overwhelmingly by commercial vessels: China built over 1,000 ocean-going commercial ships in 2024 versus five built in the US.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Signals a structural, decades-long US industrial deficit concentrated in commercial shipbuilding that reshoring/defense-tech plays like Saronic are positioned to address.

insights.claim: Narrowed to pure military vessels (destroyers, cruisers, aircraft carriers), the China-US shipbuilding gap shrinks to roughly 6-to-1 or 7-to-1, with China launching about 30 military ships a year versus 5-10 for the US.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: The real US vulnerability is commercial shipbuilding capacity, not just warship counts -- investors should track commercial shipbuilding revival, not only defense-prime contracts.
insights.quote: So, 6 to 1, 7 to 1, somewhere in there.

insights.claim: The US Navy's fleet has shrunk to around 290 ships even though Congress set a statutory minimum of 355 ships in 2018; in 2024 the Navy revised its own target upward to 381 ships, excluding unmanned vessels.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A widening, rising-target shortfall against a shrinking fleet creates durable multi-decade demand for both traditional and autonomous shipbuilders.

insights.claim: China controls 57% of total global commercial shipbuilding capacity and is expanding dominance by fully subsidizing construction, raw materials, labor, and shipyard financing to undercut world prices.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: State-subsidized overcapacity is a persistent price-suppression mechanism -- any Western shipbuilding turnaround thesis has to win on scale/autonomy economics, not price alone.
insights.quote: Their entire shipbuilding industry is completely subsidized.

insights.claim: US allies South Korea and Japan -- the world's second- and third-largest shipbuilders -- are increasingly sourcing modules and labor from China for their own commercial shipbuilding, creating dependency on the very rival the US is trying to out-produce.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Allied shipbuilding capacity is not a clean substitute for Chinese capacity due to upstream supply-chain dependency -- a risk factor for any 'friend-shoring' shipbuilding thesis.

insights.claim: Mavrookas warns that in a Taiwan Strait conflict, China's shipbuilding capacity advantage would let it outproduce the rest of the world combined in wartime ship replacement.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Reinforces the strategic case for prioritizing scalable, low-cost autonomous shipbuilding as an attrition hedge, supporting continued government and private capital flow into the sector.
insights.quote: China can outproduce the rest of the world in terms of ships.

insights.claim: The Department of War's FY26 budget is about $1 trillion against a presidential request of $1.5 trillion, and only about 1% of that budget is currently allocated to autonomy programs.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A 1% autonomy allocation against a stated national priority signals large headroom for budget reallocation toward autonomous defense-tech vendors like Saronic over the coming years.

insights.claim: Aircraft carrier cost estimates rose from a quoted $13 billion to $19 billion (the latter figure cited by the sitting president at a public event days apart), illustrating uncontrolled cost inflation in legacy shipbuilding programs.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Legacy platform cost inflation strengthens the political and budgetary case for lower-cost autonomous alternatives, a tailwind for vendors like Saronic.
insights.quote: I was actually quoting $13 billion for an aircraft carrier, and I was at an event where the president spoke just last week, and he quoted $19 billion.

insights.claim: The Navy's 30-year plan to grow the fleet from 290 to 381 ships is projected to cost $1.2 trillion, and Mavrookas is openly skeptical the country can even execute that plan as designed.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Execution risk on a trillion-dollar legacy shipbuilding plan creates room for lower-cost private/autonomous alternatives to capture share of the effective budget.
insights.quote: That'll cost $1.2 trillion if we can even execute as a country in the first place on that plan.

insights.claim: Concrete policy catalysts behind the shipbuilding buildout include a presidential maritime executive order, a maritime action plan, and the SHIPS Act moving through Congress, alongside the DIU rapid-acquisition process that let Saronic land a multi-hundred-million-dollar Navy contract in December 2025.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A trackable policy-to-revenue pipeline: legislative/executive catalysts are already converting into large, dated contract awards for autonomous shipbuilders.

insights.claim: Saronic is valued at over $9 billion after raising a cumulative $2.6 billion in venture capital, with its latest major capital commitment being a $3 billion investment in its Port Alpha shipyard program.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Places Saronic among the best-capitalized private defense-tech companies, giving it the capital advantage needed to build ahead of confirmed government demand relative to smaller competitors.

insights.claim: Saronic's Corsair platform won a multi-hundred-million-dollar Navy contract announced in December 2025, secured through the Defense Innovation Unit's (DIU) rapid-acquisition solicitation process rather than traditional slow procurement.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated revenue contract validates the 'invest ahead of demand' model and shows DIU as a viable fast lane converting defense-tech prototypes into government revenue.

insights.claim: Saronic's planned Port Arthur/Brownsville, Texas shipyard is projected to create 10,000 jobs and generate a $160 billion regional economic impact over the next 10 years, funded by billions of dollars of private investment.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: The scale of a single private shipbuilder's claimed regional economic impact signals the magnitude of capital now flowing into US shipbuilding reshoring -- a jobs/economic catalyst worth tracking regionally.
insights.quote: we're going to have a $160 billion economic impact in Brownsville, Texas

insights.claim: Saronic was founded in 2022 out of ABC's 'Build' venture program, and its lead investors across rounds include ABC, Caffeinated Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Al Gore's fund, and Kleiner Perkins, which led the most recent funding round.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Maps the cap table of a leading maritime defense-tech company, useful for tracking which funds are positioned to benefit from a future Saronic exit or follow-on rounds.

insights.claim: Saronic's product line scales by size and mission: Corsair and Mirage are smaller autonomous surface vessels already fielded, Marauder is a larger autonomous ship capable of weapons launches, and Port Alpha targets large-scale commercial and defense shipbuilding.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: The incremental product ladder (small to large, defense to dual-use) is the operating playbook Saronic used to build a track record and raise capital -- a repeatable template to screen other defense-tech shipbuilders against.

insights.claim: Mavrookas argues autonomy simplifies ship design because crew accommodations are no longer required, which enables faster, lower-cost production at scale and opens markets that were not previously commercially viable.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: This is the core economic thesis for autonomous shipbuilding: removing the human-crew constraint is what unlocks manufacturing scale and lower unit costs versus legacy shipbuilding.

insights.claim: Saronic and Castellian (a containerized hypersonic missile company run by CEO Brian) self-funded and organized a joint test to launch a hypersonic missile off Saronic's autonomous Marauder vessel, expecting to beat the Navy's own hypersonic test from a manned vessel.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Shows private capital and cross-startup collaboration outpacing government-run weapons testing timelines -- a live catalyst to watch for a hypersonic-from-autonomous-ship test result.
insights.quote: going to be able to launch a hypersonic missile off of the back of Marauder, which is an autonomous ship, before the Navy completes their first test of a hypersonic missile off of a manned vessel.

insights.claim: The number of companies that are prime defense contractors (contracting directly with the government) fell from roughly 55-60 in 1993 to about five today after decades of Pentagon-driven consolidation; Mavrookas predicts five to ten new large, impactful primes will emerge over the next five to ten years.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable prediction (5-10 new primes in 5-10 years) gives investors a shortlist framework -- Saronic, Anduril, Palantir, SpaceX-style companies -- for identifying the next winners in defense-tech venture and public markets.
insights.quote: I think you'll see five to 10 really like big impactful companies scale over the next five to 10 years.

insights.claim: Mavrookas frames Saronic, alongside Anduril, Palantir, and SpaceX, as part of a cohort proving an alternative to traditional cost-plus government contracting by investing their own capital first and demonstrating capability before the government commits funding.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: The 'invest ahead of demand' model is becoming the recognized playbook in defense-tech investing -- a differentiator investors can screen for in new defense-tech deals versus legacy primes.

insights.claim: Mavrookas argues the decline of the US commercial shipbuilding industry, not just naval budgets, is the root cause of the shipbuilding crisis, because commercial order volume is what sustains the supply chain and skilled workforce defense shipbuilding also depends on.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Fixing US shipbuilding requires rebuilding commercial order volume, not just defense contracts -- makes Saronic's Port Alpha push into commercial vessels arguably more structurally important than its Navy contracts.
insights.quote: That's the first step into how this shipbuilding fiasco even started was the commercial shipbuilding industry kind of went away and the supply chain and the workforce went with it.

insights.claim: Saronic is extending its autonomy platform into commercial applications by mission tier: Corsair for port/harbor security work with the Coast Guard, Marauder for commercial logistics operations, and Port Alpha for autonomy in container ships, tankers, and roll-on/roll-off vessels.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: A dual-use commercial revenue base reduces reliance on lumpy government contracts and could make Saronic comparable to a diversified industrial company rather than a pure defense contractor.

insights.claim: Mavrookas cites World War II logistics ships as historical precedent for why commercial vessel types like tankers and roll-on/roll-off ships are militarily critical -- without them the US cannot resupply forces during a prolonged conflict.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Frames commercial-vessel autonomy (tankers, RoRo ships) as a national-security-relevant category, not just a commercial revenue play, potentially justifying future defense-linked demand for that segment.

insights.claim: Mavrookas left an 11-year career in the Navy SEAL Teams (2004-2015, the last five years on SEAL Team Six) and five years at private equity firm Vista Equity Partners before founding Saronic in 2022, choosing to bet on defense tech he was passionate about rather than continue in finance.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: An elite-military-operator-plus-PE-investor pedigree is an increasingly common founder pattern in top defense-tech startups, useful context for team diligence.

insights.claim: Mavrookas notes the lesser-known fact that the US Army operates more boats than the Navy, and Saronic deliberately builds for all military branches (Navy, Army, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and Air Force combat search-and-rescue support) plus international allies, rather than treating the Navy as its sole customer.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: Signals a broader addressable market than Navy contracts alone -- multi-branch and allied demand diversification reduces single-customer/program concentration risk.
insights.quote: The Army actually has more boats than the Navy does.

insights.claim: Mavrookas's stated highest-conviction view is that the entire global maritime industry -- not just the defense sector -- will become centered on autonomy.
insights.speaker: Dino Mavrookas, guest (CEO, Saronic)
insights.so_what: This is the founder's core long-term investment thesis: it frames Saronic as a bet on a full industry transition rather than a niche defense-tech product, relevant to evaluating the TAM assumptions behind its $9B+ valuation.
insights.quote: I do believe I'm like fully convicted in the future of not not just the defense market, but the entire maritime industry is centered around autonomy
